name: Akkbor
title: Official at King Josiah's court in Judah
summary: Achbor, son of Micaiah, was a high-ranking official in King Josiah's service in the kingdom of Judah. When the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law during restoration work in the temple around 622 BC, King Josiah sent a delegation to seek the Lord's will regarding the serious content of the book. Achbor was among those chosen who consulted the prophetess Huldah, and her words of judgment over Judah – but promise of mercy for the humble king – were brought back and sparked a thorough religious reform. In the parallel account in 2 Chronicles 34 he is called Abdon, son of Micah, which testifies to different naming traditions in the biblical sources. Achbor's son El-nathan continued the family's role in the kingdom's service as an official under King Jehoiakim.

keyEvents.title: The Book of the Law Found in the Temple
keyEvents.description: During repairs to the temple, the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law. The discovery was reported to King Josiah through the scribe Shaphan, and its contents deeply shook the king. This set in motion the events that led to Akbor's involvement.

keyEvents.title: Akbor is sent as part of the delegation
keyEvents.description: King Josiah sent Akbor along with the priest Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, the scribe Shaphan, and Asaiah to inquire of the Lord about the contents of the Book of the Law that had been found.

keyEvents.title: The prophetess Huldah is consulted
keyEvents.description: The delegation, including Akbor, sought out the prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem. She gave them a solemn message from the Lord concerning coming judgment on Judah because of the people's persistent apostasy and idolatry.

keyEvents.title: Huldah's Message of Mercy to Josiah
keyEvents.description: Huldah also delivered a message specifically to King Josiah: because he had humbled himself before the Lord and torn his clothes in grief over the people's sin, judgment would not come during his lifetime.

keyEvents.title: The Delegation's Message Leads to Reform
keyEvents.description: After the delegation brought back Huldah's prophecy, King Josiah gathered the people and launched a thorough religious reform involving a solemn covenant renewal and the removal of idolatry throughout Judah.

keyEvents.title: The Parallel Account in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: In 2 Chronicles, Akbor is referred to as Abdon son of Mica and is mentioned in the same event as a member of the delegation sent to the prophetess Huldah.

keyEvents.title: Akbor's Son Elkanah Serves under Jehoiakim
keyEvents.description: Akbor's son Elkanah served as an official under King Jehoiakim. He is mentioned in connection with the retrieval of the prophet Uriah from Egypt (Jer 26:22) and later among those who heard Jeremiah's scroll read and urged the king not to burn it (Jer 36:12,25).

versions.summary: Akbor, son of Micaiah, was one of the prominent officials at King Josiah's court in Judah. He was sent along with other servants to consult the prophetess Huldah after the Book of the Law was found in the temple. He played an important role in the religious reform movement during Josiah's reign.
versions.title: Envoy for King Josiah
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Messenger for King Josiah' is clear, but 'Official at King Josiah's court' would be more precise, since he was a permanent official and not merely a messenger on one occasion.; [major] The role 'leader' is imprecise for Akbor. He was primarily an official/courtier at King Josiah's court. The roles should include 'official' or 'courtier' and possibly 'messenger' to reflect his actual function.; [minor] The first key event concerns the general discovery of the Book of the Law, but Akbor is not directly mentioned in 2 Kings 22:8-10. Akbor's role begins in verse 12. This is good background information, but it should be clarified that this is the context for his mission, not an event he directly participated in.; [minor] Akbor is not explicitly named in 2 Kings 23:1-3 as a participant in the actual implementation of the reform. It is a reasonable conclusion that the delegation brought back the message, but this should be phrased more cautiously.; [minor] The identification of Akbor (son of Micaiah) with the father of Elnatan (son of Akbor) in Jeremiah 26:22 and 36:12,25 is a common and reasonable identification, but it is worth noting that this is not 100% certain, as there may have been several people named Akbor.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological aspects to illuminate: the meaning of the name, the historical context surrounding Josiah's reform, archaeological findings related to the period, and the parallel account in 2 Chronicles.

versions.summary: Achbor, son of Micaiah, was a prominent official at King Josiah's court in Judah. When the high priest Hilkiah found the Book of the Law in the temple around 622 BC, Achbor was appointed as part of the delegation sent to consult the prophetess Huldah about the book's contents. Huldah's prophecy of coming judgment on Judah, yet mercy for the humble Josiah, was brought back and triggered a widespread religious reform. In the parallel account in 2 Chronicles he is called Abdon, son of Micah. His son Elnatan later served as an official under King Jehoiakim.
versions.title: Official at King Josiah's Court
versions.reason: [minor] The order of the names in the delegation is somewhat imprecise. According to 2 Kings 22:12, it is Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan (the scribe), and Asaiah. 'Shaphan' should be mentioned as the scribe, not merely as a name in the list, to avoid confusion with Ahikam son of Shaphan.; [minor] The summary is good, but the phrase 'was appointed as part of the delegation' is somewhat passive. More precisely, it was the king who sent the entire delegation after hearing the words of the Book of the Law. A slightly more active formulation would strengthen the text.; [minor] The event 'The Book of the Law is found' primarily concerns the actual discovery (v. 8) and its reporting to the king. Verse 10 deals with Shaphan reading the book to the king. Achbor is not mentioned until verse 12. The event is relevant as context, but it should be considered whether these verses are the most precise for showing Achbor's involvement. They do, however, work well as background information.; [minor] Jeremiah 26:22 mentions 'Elnathan son of Achbor' in connection with bringing the prophet Uriah from Egypt, not directly with the reading of the scrolls. The description mixes two separate events (Jer 26:22 and Jer 36:12,25). It is correct that both references mention Elnathan, but the description should more clearly distinguish between the two events.

versions.reason: [minor] In 2 Kgs 22:12, the members of the delegation are mentioned. The list includes 'Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan (the scribe), and Asaiah'. The description says 'the scribe Shaphan', but it could also be noted that Ahikam is the son of Shaphan. Shaphan had already read the Book of the Law to the king. The wording is acceptable but could have been slightly more precise.; [minor] The description uses the term 'chain reaction' – this is a somewhat unusual word. 'Chain of events' or 'course of events' would be more natural Norwegian.; [minor] The summary is good and informative. footnotes.text: The name Akbor (Hebrew: עַכְבּוֹר, ʿAkhbor) means 'mouse'. Animal names were common as personal names in ancient Israel and the wider Semitic Middle East. A similar naming pattern is found in Ugaritic and Akkadian texts.

Josiah's religious reform around 622 BC is considered one of the best-documented events in Judah's history. The discovery of the Book of the Law in the temple is linked by many scholars to an early form of Deuteronomy or parts of it. The reform included, among other things, the removal of idolatry and the centralization of worship in Jerusalem.

The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 34:20 calls Akbor 'Abdon son of Mica'. This is most likely the same person, with variations in name forms between Kings and Chronicles—a well-known phenomenon in biblical literature that may be due to different source and manuscript traditions.

Several seals and bullae (clay seal impressions) from the 7th and early 6th centuries BCE have been found archaeologically in the Jerusalem area, some bearing names that match officials mentioned in biblical texts from the time of Josiah and Jehoiakim. Among them is a bulla attributed to 'Gemariah son of Shaphan,' another person mentioned in the book of Jeremiah. This confirms the existence of a well-developed bureaucratic system in the late kingdom of Judah.

The fact that King Josiah sent a delegation of high-ranking men to consult a female prophet (Huldah) is remarkable and shows that women could hold recognized prophetic roles in ancient Israel, on par with Miriam (Exod 15:20) and Deborah (Judg 4:4).

Elnatan son of Akbor served as an official under King Jehoiakim (c. 609–598 BCE). He is mentioned in Jeremiah 26:22 in connection with the retrieval of the prophet Uriah from Egypt, and in Jeremiah 36:12,25 as one of those who heard Jeremiah's scroll read aloud and urged the king not to burn it. The fact that both father and son served as officials suggests a prominent official family in the late kingdom of Judah.

In rabbinic tradition, Josiah's reform has been seen as a high point in Judah's spiritual history. The Talmud (Megillah 14b) discusses the prophetess Huldah and asks why the delegation sought her out instead of the prophet Jeremiah. One explanation is that women were traditionally regarded as more merciful, and it was hoped for a milder message.
